meta.title: Who really said "People who lean on logic and philosophy and rational exposition end by starving the best part of the mind"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yeats scholar Neil Mann traces this line to the poet’s father, painter John Butler Yeats, in a 1906 letter to his son. Right family, wrong Yeats.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'People who lean on logic and philosophy and rational exposition end by starving the best part of the mind'?
meta.ogDescription: Not the poet. A Yeats scholar puts this line in a 1906 letter from John Butler Yeats to his son W. B. Yeats. Right family, wrong Yeats.

answer.label: Not W. B. Yeats — actually John Butler Yeats
answer.authorDates: 1839–1922 · Irish portrait painter · father of the poet
answer.sourceLine: The Yeats scholar Neil Mann, who maintains yeatsvision.com, lists this sentence among the lines wrongly hung on the poet and gives its origin as a letter from John Butler Yeats to his son, W. B. Yeats, in 1906 ↗. It is not in the poet’s own prose — neither Ideas of Good and Evil ↗ nor Essays (Macmillan, 1924) ↗ contains it — and Mann gives no volume or page, so the letter itself remains unread here.

source.excerpt: People who lean on logic and philosophy and rational exposition end by starving the best part of the mind.
trail: Neil Mann — who has edited volumes of essays on A Vision and written A Reader’s Guide to Yeats’s “A Vision” — audited a “Top Ten Yeats Quotes” list published for the poet’s birthday and judged only four of the ten authentic. Against this one he wrote: “John Butler Yeats to his son, W. B. Yeats, in 1906” ↗.

It is in neither of the poet’s two main prose collections. Searching the full text of Ideas of Good and Evil ↗ returns no “starving”, no “rational exposition” and no “lean on logic”; a full-text search of Essays (Macmillan, 1924) ↗ returns no hit for “starving” at all. That is two books, not the whole corpus — it is Mann’s positive identification of the father, not this search, that settles who wrote the line.

The father’s letters reached print in stages, and the earliest public selection cannot cover 1906: the editor’s note to Passages from the Letters of John Butler Yeats ↗ (Cuala Press, 1917), chosen by Ezra Pound, states that the letters it draws on “were written to W. B. Yeats between 1911 and 1916” — and the sentence is not in that volume.
Every popular source that credits the poet cites nothing. Goodreads ↗ gives it to “William Butler Yeats” with a tag and no work, under its own notice that community-added quotes are not verified.
source.excerptNote: No fuller context is quoted anywhere reachable: Mann prints the sentence alone, and the surrounding paragraph of the 1906 letter is not reproduced in any source located here.

source.rightsNote: The sentence comes from private family correspondence, and no source consulted here identifies which published volume first printed it — so its copyright status cannot be settled. It is not in the 1917 Cuala Press selection of John Butler Yeats’s letters; the standard collected edition, J. B. Yeats: Letters to His Son W. B. Yeats and Others, 1869–1922 ↗, edited by Joseph Hone, was published by Faber and Faber in 1944, and a first printing of that date would be in copyright in the United States. Treated as uncertain rather than public domain.

author.name: John Butler Yeats
author.heading: The father who wrote the line
author.metaLine: 1839–1922 · Irish portrait painter · father of W. B. and Jack B. Yeats
author.bio: John Butler Yeats trained as a lawyer, took up painting in 1867, and spent his life as a portrait painter and an inexhaustible letter-writer — father of the poet W. B. Yeats and the painter Jack B. Yeats. In 1907 he sailed to New York with his daughter Lily and never returned to Ireland, dying there in 1922. His talk-on-paper made enough of an impression that Ezra Pound culled a Cuala Press volume from it in 1917, warning in his editor’s note that snatching at “salient thoughts” risked making a preacher of a man whose letters had only “the air of leisure.”

misattribution.heading: Right family, wrong Yeats
misattribution.intro: This is not a stranger’s line pinned on a famous name. It is a father’s line pinned on his more famous son — the easiest kind of slip to make, and the hardest to notice, because both men are “Yeats” and both wrote well.

items.why: Quote sites give it to the poet with a topic tag and nothing else — Goodreads ↗ lists no work at all. Neil Mann marks it false and puts it in the father’s 1906 letter to his son.

On the same list Mann flags “Happiness is neither virtue nor pleasure nor this thing nor that but simply growth” as John Butler Yeats again, writing to a Miss Grierson in 1909, slightly adapted ↗. Two of the ten lines on that birthday Top Ten list turn out to be his father’s.

The most-shared “Yeats” line of all — “Education is not the filling of a pail, but the lighting of a fire” — isn’t his either. Quote Investigator credits it to Plutarch ↗. James Johnson Sweeney’s Vision and Image (1968) gave that line to Plutarch and printed it beside a genuine Yeats sentence, and both Quote Investigator and Neil Mann suggest a reader misreading that juxtaposition is how it drifted — the earliest ascription to Yeats that QI can date is a 1987 quotation dictionary.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought really is a Yeats thought — just the wrong Yeats. Neil Mann places it in a 1906 letter from the painter John Butler Yeats to his son ↗, and it appears in neither Ideas of Good and Evil ↗ nor Essays ↗.

context.heading: Why this one is so easy to get wrong
lead: Of all the misattributions that gather around a famous name, the family kind is the most forgivable. John Butler Yeats wrote to his son constantly, in a voice built for quoting — opinionated, aphoristic, arriving in short hard sentences. When a phrase from that correspondence escapes into circulation with only the surname attached, the poet is who readers picture.

Ezra Pound saw the risk as early as 1917. Introducing his Cuala Press selection from the father’s letters, he worried that by “snatching at salient thoughts” he would make the man look “hurried, or even sententious,” when in the letters themselves “there is only the air of leisure.” A century of copy-paste quoting has done exactly what Pound feared — and then handed the results to the wrong Yeats.
detailsBody: Neil Mann gives the year and the correspondents but no volume or page, and no source located here reproduces the paragraph the sentence sits in. The line is not in the 1917 Cuala Press selection, whose letters run only from 1911 to 1916. Where it was first printed — and therefore whether it is out of copyright — remains open.
If you can point to the letter in a published edition of John Butler Yeats’s correspondence, with a date and a page, that would close the last gap on this page.

sourcesVerified.claim: Neil Mann's post lists this quote as a false attribution to W. B. Yeats (item 9 of a Top Ten list) and gives its origin as "John Butler Yeats to his son, W. B. Yeats, in 1906"; it also flags the "Happiness is neither virtue nor pleasure" line as John Butler Yeats to Miss Grierson in 1909, slightly adapted. Post dated Friday, October 5, 2018; the author bio states he edited W. B. Yeats's "A Vision": Explications and Contexts and wrote A Reader's Guide to Yeats's "A Vision".
Wikiquote's W. B. Yeats page does not contain the sentence "People who lean on logic and philosophy and rational exposition end by starving the best part of the mind" in any section.
The complete text of W. B. Yeats's Ideas of Good and Evil contains no occurrence of "starving", "rational exposition" or "lean on logic" (verified by downloading and grepping the full HTML text).
Wikisource's edition of Ideas of Good and Evil is set from the A. H. Bullen, London, MCMIII (1903) printing.
The item is W. B. Yeats, Essays, London: Macmillan and co., 1924; an Internet Archive full-text search of the item for "starving" returns 0 matches.

The item is Passages from the Letters of John Butler Yeats, Selected by Ezra Pound, Cuala Press, 1917; its editor's note states the letters "were written to W. B. Yeats between 1911 and 1916" and worries that "snatching at salient thoughts" may make the author seem "hurried, or even sententious" when in the letters "there is only the air of leisure". The full text contains no occurrence of "starving", "rational", or "lean on/upon".

Goodreads presents the quote attributed to W. B. Yeats with a 'philosophy' tag, no work or source citation, and a notice that quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.

Quote Investigator concludes that "Education is not the filling of a pail, but the lighting of a fire" is properly credited to Plutarch. James Johnson Sweeney's Vision and Image (1968) printed that line credited to Plutarch beside a genuine Yeats quotation ("Culture does not consist in acquiring opinions but in getting rid of them"); QI offers the transfer only as a general mechanism ("A reader sometimes inadvertently transfers the ascription of one quote to a contiguous quote") and dates the earliest ascription of the line to Yeats to the 1987 Barnes & Noble Book of Quotations.

John Butler Yeats was born 16 March 1839 and died 3 February 1922 in New York City; he took up painting in 1867; his children included W. B. Yeats and Jack B. Yeats; in 1907 he travelled to New York with his daughter Lily and never returned to Ireland; J.B. Yeats Letters to his son W. B. Yeats and Others was published in 1944, edited by Joseph Hone.
